did_you_know.text: The song begins with “Then,” showing that the people respond to their rescue with song. Moses and the Israelites sing together, making it a communal song rather than a solo.
“Yah” is a poetic shortened form of God’s name. It also appears in “Hallelujah,” meaning “Praise Yah.”
The word “ned” means a heap or mound, so the waters are pictured as being piled up like a wall. This is poetic imagery, not a scientific description of frozen water.
The question “Who is like You?” became a familiar part of Jewish prayer, especially in the “Mi Khamokha” passage recited after the Shema.
Philistia refers to the region of the Philistines, who lived mainly along the southern coastal plain of Canaan. The song therefore imagines the reaction of peoples along Israel’s route.

The verbs “You will bring them” and “You will plant them” are in the future, even though the song has already described the sea crossing. The song moves from past rescue to hope for settlement and a sanctuary.
A “tof” was a frame drum, and “mecholot” were dances. Miriam and the women express their joy through music, movement, and public leadership.
The name “Marah” is related to the Hebrew word for “bitter.” It is a biblical wordplay in which the place-name explains the Israelites’ experience there.
At the end of the verse, God is called “your healer.” Medical language is used to describe God’s relationship to the people’s health and protection.
